question.text: Scenario: Vikram (age 32) is a software engineer earning Rs. 18,00,000 per annum. His wife Priya (age 30) also works and earns Rs. 8,00,000 per annum. They have one child aged 2 years, who is their only dependent. They own a house valued at Rs. 40,00,000 with an outstanding home loan of Rs. 15,00,000. Their current investments include: Rs. 5,00,000 in bank fixed deposits, Rs. 3,00,000 in equity mutual funds, Rs. 2,00,000 in PPF, and an emergency fund of Rs. 1,50,000. Vikram has long investment experience and holds investments across a wide range of products; he reports being comfortable holding investments through a 30%+ market drawdown. Their financial goals are: child's higher education (16 years away), retirement (28 years away), and a car upgrade (2 years away). Question 2 of 5: The NISM Series X-B workbook (p. 416) presents a model portfolio of 50% equity / 20% sector / 10% gold ETF / 10% debt / 10% liquid as the illustrative high-risk allocation for a young, no-dependent investor with high risk profile. Among the four allocations below, which is the SAME high-risk model portfolio as illustrated on p. 416? (Note: the workbook states model portfolios are illustrative and must be tweaked for the specific investor; this question asks ONLY which option matches the p. 416 illustration, not which is suitable for Vikram.)

answer.text: 15% equity index, 5% gold, 35% debt hybrid/MIS/SCSS, 30% debt/FD, 15% liquid
50% equity, 20% sector, 10% gold ETF, 10% debt, 10% liquid

explanation.text: The Logic: NISM Series X-B workbook p. 416 explicitly illustrates the high-risk model allocation as 50% equity / 20% sector / 10% gold ETF / 10% debt / 10% liquid (~70% equity exposure). Option B reproduces that allocation exactly, so it is the uniquely correct answer to the source-matching question. The Trap: Option C matches a moderate-risk young-married-family model. Option D is a more conservative model. Option A is the illustrative allocation for a couple in their 70s. Each is "close" to some part of Vikram's profile (he has one dependent, he has a long horizon, etc.), and the audit flagged that under the original wording (asking which allocation is "most appropriate" for Vikram), option C also became defensible because the workbook itself says model portfolios are illustrative and must be tweaked when the investor has dependents. Note: The original stem asked which allocation was MOST APPROPRIATE for Vikram — the workbook's p. 416 high-risk model assumes a young call-centre/BPO employee with NO dependents, while Vikram is married with one dependent. The stem has been narrowed to ask only which option matches the p. 416 high-risk model portfolio as illustrated. On that source-matching basis, option B is unambiguously correct.
